paragraphs.heading: What marble is
paragraphs.text: Marble is a metamorphic rock built from carbonate minerals, most often calcite (CaCO₃) or dolomite (CaMg(CO₃)₂), which have recrystallized under heat and pressure. Its texture is crystalline. It usually has no layering, though some marbles do. It comes from sedimentary carbonate rocks, most commonly limestone or dolomite, that have gone through metamorphism.

paragraphs.heading: What metamorphism does
paragraphs.text: During metamorphism the original carbonate grains recrystallize, some more and some less. The marble that results is typically a mosaic of carbonate crystals locked into one another. The starting rock is called the protolith. The textures and structures it had as a sediment have typically been altered or wiped out.

paragraphs.heading: Where the veins come from
paragraphs.text: Pure white marble comes from a very pure limestone or dolomite, one with little silicate in it. The swirls and veins seen in many coloured marbles are usually due to mineral impurities. Clay, silt, sand, chert and iron oxides are examples. These sat in the limestone as grains or layers. The strong heat and pressure of metamorphism set them moving and recrystallized them. A green colour often comes from serpentine, which results from a limestone or dolomite that was rich in magnesium and carried silica impurities.

paragraphs.heading: Why sculptors choose it
paragraphs.text: White marble has been prized for sculpture since classical times. It is soft, which made it easier to carve, it is fairly even throughout, and it resists shattering fairly well. Calcite also has a low index of refraction, so light travels 12.7 to 38 millimeters into the stone before it is scattered back out. That gives marble sculpture a waxy look and a lifelike luster. It is the reason many sculptors have preferred marble for the human form, and still do.

paragraphs.heading: One word, two meanings
paragraphs.text: To a geologist, marble means limestone that has been metamorphosed. Stonemasons use the word more loosely, and include limestone that has not been metamorphosed. In the building stone trade, marble can mean any crystalline calcitic rock, and some non-calcitic ones, that is useful as building stone. Tennessee marble is an example. It is really a dense, granular, fossil-bearing limestone, which geologists call the Holston Formation.

paragraphs.heading: Damage from acid
paragraphs.text: Marble statues, gravestones and other structures that stand outdoors are damaged by acid rain. The harm can come through carbonation, through sulfation, or through a "black-crust", a build-up of calcium sulphate, nitrates and carbon particles. Vinegar and other acidic solutions should not be used to clean marble products.
